As time passes, soil builds up and more niches become available, so slower-growing species that couldn't establish early on are able to move in, and the community becomes more diverse and more even.

Richness alone just counts how many species are present, but says nothing about how individuals are distributed among those species. Early-successional environments favor r-selected species: fast growth rates, high seed/spore output, good dispersal (e.g., wind-blown seeds), and tolerance of the harsh, high-light, low-nutrient conditions right after a fire. These traits let a few species colonize and dominate quickly while competitors haven't arrived yet. Over time, as these pioneer species alter the environment (building soil organic matter, creating shade, changing nutrient availability), conditions become suitable for a wider range of species with different resource requirements. This niche differentiation, combined with the pioneers no longer having a competitive advantage once conditions change, allows more species to coexist by partitioning resources rather than all competing for the exact same ones, producing the higher diversity seen later in succession.
